stageDescription: Why governance exists, and how risk, controls, accountability and oversight connect.
title: Governance operating model

stops.title: In one line
stops.contentMd:
## In one line

The AI governance operating model is how an organisation actually runs AI governance day to day: who decides what, through which process, with which documents, committees, tools and people.

## Explained like you're 10

How a school runs trips safely.

- **Rule book:** what kind of trips are allowed. (AI policy)
- **List of every trip:** nobody runs a secret trip. (AI inventory)
- **Permission slip:** you must ask before planning a trip. (Intake)
- **Risk level:** a museum visit is easy; a mountain hike needs more checks. (Risk tiering)
- **Trip leader:** one teacher responsible for each trip. (System owner)
- **Head teacher's approval** for risky trips. (Steering committee)
- **Spot-checks** by an inspector. (Internal audit)
- **Training** so every teacher knows the rules. (AI literacy)
- **Report after each trip:** what went well and wrong. (Monitoring and incidents)

An operating model makes the rule book actually work, every time, without the head teacher having to check everything personally.

## Why this is what consultants actually deliver

Look at the EY JD again: "design, develop and operationalise the enterprise AI governance framework, including governance structures, policies, standards, procedures, and clearly defined roles, responsibilities and decision rights", plus "establish an AI Governance and Ethics Steering Committee" and "awareness programmes and training". That's the operating model.

Frameworks like ISO 42001 and NIST say *what* must exist. The operating model is the client-specific answer to *how*: which committee, which form, which tool, which person. Clients pay for that answer.

**The test of a good operating model:** a new AI use case appears on Monday. Does everyone know where it goes, who assesses it, who can approve it, and how long that takes? If not, people will route around governance.

## Level 1: The building blocks

| Block | What it is | Approved by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Principles | The organisation's responsible AI values | Board |
| AI policy | The "musts": scope, definition of AI, roles, risk appetite, prohibited uses | Board or board risk committee |
| Standards | Minimum requirements by topic: GenAI use, model validation, third-party AI, monitoring | AI committee or CRO |
| Procedures | How-to steps: intake form, assessment workflow, approval gates | Function heads |
| AI inventory | Every AI system: owner, purpose, vendor, data, tier, status, review date | Maintained by the AI governance office |
| Intake and triage | The front door: every new use case is registered and tiered | AI governance office |
| Risk tiering criteria | Rules that set how much scrutiny each use case gets | AI committee |
| Lifecycle gates | Checkpoints from idea to retirement, scaled by tier | AI committee |
| Assessment templates | Combined impact assessment (DPIA, FRIA, AI impact) | AI governance office with privacy |
| Control library | Controls mapped to risks and frameworks | 2nd line |
| Monitoring and incidents | KRIs, reporting, AI incident process | System owners, reported to committee |
| Training | Role-based AI literacy | HR with the AI governance office |

**Why policy and standards are separate:** the policy should rarely change and needs board approval. Thresholds and technical requirements change fast. Put them in standards so you aren't back at the board every quarter.

### Example tiering criteria

| Tier | Typical features | Scrutiny |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tier 1, high | Decides or strongly influences outcomes for customers or staff; regulated area; sensitive data; customer-facing GenAI | Full assessment, validation, 2LOD approval, committee sign-off, monthly monitoring |
| Tier 2, medium | Internal use influencing decisions; personal data; moderate scale | Standard assessment, owner and 2LOD sign-off, quarterly monitoring |
| Tier 3, low | Internal productivity, no personal data, human always reviews | Short checklist, owner sign-off, annual review |

[embedded content: AI governance structure · hub-and-spoke with three lines\]

Only Tier 1 cases climb to the committee. Everything else is handled by champions and the hub, which is what keeps governance fast.

## Level 2: Operating model choices and RACI

### Three models

| Model | How it works | Strength | Weakness | Fits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Centralised | One AI governance office does all assessments and approvals | Consistent | Becomes a bottleneck | Small firms, early stage |
| Federated | Each business unit governs its own AI | Fast, close to the business | Inconsistent; gaps between units | Highly diverse groups |
| **Hub-and-spoke** | A central office sets standards, tools and approves high-risk cases; trained AI champions in each unit run assessments | Consistent and scalable | Needs good champions and training | Most large enterprises |

Recommend hub-and-spoke for most large clients, but justify it by their size, maturity and how many AI use cases they have.

### Sample RACI

R = responsible, A = accountable, C = consulted, I = informed.

| Activity | System owner | Data science or tech | AI governance office | Legal and privacy | Security | AI committee |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Register use case | A | R | C | I | I | I |
| Risk tiering | A | C | R | C | C | I |
| Impact assessment | A | C | R | R | C | I |
| Validation and testing | A | R | C | I | R | I |
| Approve Tier 1 deployment | C | C | R | C | C | A |
| Ongoing monitoring | A | R | C | I | R | I |
| Accept above-appetite risk | R | C | C | C | C | A |

### Decision rights

Write down, per tier, **who can approve, who can accept residual risk, and who must be consulted.** Most governance failures aren't missing policies; they're nobody knowing who could say no.

## Level 3: The steering committee

### Charter contents

| Element | Typical content |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and mandate | Oversee AI risk and responsible AI; delegated from the board or board risk committee |
| Chair | A senior executive, often the CRO, COO or Chief Data Officer |
| Members | Business heads, technology, data, risk, compliance, legal, privacy, security, HR; internal audit attends as observer |
| Quorum and voting | Minimum attendance; how decisions are made when members disagree |
| Decision rights | Approve AI policy and standards; approve Tier 1 use cases; accept above-appetite risk; resolve escalations; **say no on ethical grounds** |
| Cadence | Monthly at launch, then quarterly, with a fast route for urgent approvals |
| Escalation | To the board risk committee |

### Standing agenda and reporting pack

1. Inventory changes: new, changed and retired systems
2. Tier 1 approvals requested
3. Risk heatmap and KRI trends
4. Open issues and overdue actions
5. Incidents and lessons learned
6. Accepted risks nearing expiry
7. Regulatory horizon scan
8. Programme roadmap progress

### Why "ethics" belongs in the name

Some uses are legal and within appetite but still wrong for the brand, such as inferring customers' emotions to push sales. Give the committee explicit authority to refuse on ethical grounds, or it will defer to legality every time.

### Two ways committees fail

- **Rubber stamp:** approves everything, never challenges. Sign: no project has ever been changed or stopped.
- **Bottleneck:** everything waits for a monthly meeting. Fix: tiering, so only Tier 1 reaches the committee, plus a fast-track route.

## Level 4: Maturity assessments and roadmaps

A gap assessment asks "is each requirement met?" A maturity assessment asks "how embedded and repeatable is it?" Clients need both: gaps for compliance, maturity to plan investment.

### Method

1. **Scope:** frameworks (ISO 42001, NIST, EU AI Act, sector rules), entities, systems.
2. **Evidence:** documents, interviews across business, tech, risk, legal, privacy, security and audit, plus a **walkthrough of 2-3 live use cases** end to end. Walkthroughs reveal the gap between policy and practice.
3. **Score** each domain on a 1-5 scale against criteria agreed in advance, citing evidence.
4. **Root causes:** group symptoms. "No assessments done" is often really "no owner and no intake trigger".
5. **Roadmap** with owners and costs, and a current-vs-target heatmap for the committee.

### Maturity scale

| Level | Description |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Initial | Ad hoc; no inventory; governed only if someone happens to ask |
| 2 Developing | Policy drafted; some assessments; inconsistent across units |
| 3 Defined | Documented framework applied consistently; inventory complete; roles clear |
| 4 Managed | Measured with KRIs; controls tested; board reporting; tooling supports it |
| 5 Optimised | Continuous improvement; incident lessons fed back; governance speeds up delivery |

### Domains to score

Strategy and leadership; policy and standards; roles and operating model; AI inventory; risk and impact assessment; data governance; lifecycle controls; monitoring and incidents; third-party AI; security; transparency; training and culture; regulatory compliance.

### Findings you can predict for most clients in 2026

- Inventory incomplete, especially AI features inside vendor software
- Policy exists but no intake trigger, so nothing forces assessment
- GenAI falls between model risk and IT risk; nobody owns it
- Strong pre-launch review, weak post-launch monitoring
- Vendor contracts lack AI clauses
- Generic awareness training only

### Roadmap shape

Quick wins (0-3 months) such as an acceptable-use policy and inventory sprint; foundations (3-9 months) such as policy, tiering, committee, assessment process; embedding and certification (9-18 months) such as monitoring, control testing, ISO 42001 readiness.

## Level 5: Adoption, training, tooling and measuring success

A framework nobody uses is the most common failure. Adoption is designed, not hoped for.

### Make the right route the easy route

- **Proportionate tiers:** low-risk tools get approved in days, not months.
- **Embed in existing processes:** intake inside procurement, project approval and the software release process, not a separate form people forget.
- **Published turnaround times** for reviews.
- **AI champions** in each business unit who know the process and help colleagues.

### Role-based training

| Audience | Content |
| --- | --- |
| All staff | Acceptable use, what not to paste into AI tools, how to register a tool, how to raise a concern |
| System owners | Their accountability, intake, tiering, what approval means |
| Builders | Lifecycle standards, documentation, testing, secure GenAI patterns |
| 2nd-line reviewers | How to challenge an assessment; evidence standards |
| Board and executives | Risk landscape, regulation, their oversight duties, questions to ask |

### Tooling

Spreadsheets work for 20 systems and fail at 200. AI governance platforms and GRC tools hold the inventory, run intake and assessment workflows, store evidence, map controls to frameworks, and produce committee reporting. You've sold one of these, so you can speak to what buyers look for.

### Measuring success

| Metric | Tells you |
| --- | --- |
| % of AI systems in the inventory with a current assessment | Coverage |
| Average days from intake to decision, by tier | Whether governance is a bottleneck |
| Unregistered tools found | Shadow AI, and whether the front door works |
| Overdue actions | Whether findings get fixed |
| AI incidents and near misses | Whether controls work |
| Training completion by role | Whether people know the rules |
| Projects changed or stopped by governance | Whether the committee has teeth |
stops.artifactPrompt: Pick an organisation you know (current or past employer). Fill in the Level 1 'building blocks' table for it as honestly as you can: for each of the 12 blocks, note whether it exists, is partial, or is missing. Then pick one missing block and write one sentence on who would need to approve it if it were built.

stops.title: Worked example: the first 90 days at a client with no AI governance
stops.contentMd:
## Worked example: the first 90 days at a client with no AI governance

Client: a mid-sized Indian private bank with about 30 AI use cases and no framework. This is the answer to "walk me through your first 90 days".

| Phase | Weeks | Activities | Deliverables |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Discover | 1-4 | Stakeholder interviews; inventory sprint including vendor AI features; maturity baseline; walkthroughs of 3 live use cases | AI inventory v1; maturity heatmap; top 10 findings |
| Quick wins | 2-4 | GenAI acceptable-use policy; interim approval route for urgent use cases | Acceptable-use policy; interim process |
| Design | 5-8 | AI policy aligned to RBI FREE-AI; tiering criteria; taxonomy mapped to enterprise risk; RACI and decision rights; committee charter; combined impact assessment template | Draft policy; tiering criteria; RACI; charter; templates |
| Pilot | 9-12 | Run the full process on 3 use cases of different tiers; refine; draft control library; training plan; roadmap | Pilot results; control library v1; training plan; 12-month roadmap; committee's first meeting |

**Principles to say out loud:** pilot before scaling; embed in existing processes; proportionality; get the committee's first decision on the record early so the framework is seen to work.
stops.artifactPrompt: Write your own first-90-days plan in the same 4-phase table (Discover, Quick wins, Design, Pilot), for a hypothetical organisation in your target industry that has no AI governance yet. Give each phase concrete weeks, activities and deliverables, the way the worked example does.

stops.title: Applied to your CV
stops.contentMd:
## Applied to your CV

| Your experience | Operating-model angle |
| --- | --- |
| Barclays 1LOD Chief Controls Office | You worked inside a mature three-lines model; you know how 1st line, 2nd line and audit interact, and where handoffs break |
| Controls forums and MI | You've prepared reporting packs for a governance forum: the same skill as an AI committee pack |
| Help Hub ownership gaps | A live example of a missing RACI: nobody owned the knowledge base |
| Thresholds set by engineering | A decision-rights failure: the wrong people made a risk decision by default |
| Selling an AI governance platform | You've seen many organisations' operating models and what tooling buyers need |

**Interview line:** "Most of my Barclays findings were operating-model failures, not technology failures: unclear ownership, decision rights sitting with the wrong team, and controls nobody had to use. That's why I'd start any engagement with the RACI and decision rights, not the policy wording."

## Free videos and courses

Suggested path: 1, then the governance units of 2, then the GOVERN section of 3.

| # | Resource | Source | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | [AI Governance in Practice Report (2024)](https://iapp.org/resources/article/at-a-glance-ai-governance-in-practice-report) | IAPP with FTI Consulting | How organisations are actually structuring AI governance. The at-a-glance infographic is free; check access to the full report |
| 2 | [Embrace responsible AI principles and practices](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/modules/embrace-responsible-ai-principles-practices) | Microsoft Learn | Units 4 and 5 cover designing and applying a governance system |
| 3 | [NIST AI RMF Playbook](https://airc.nist.gov/airmf-resources/playbook) | NIST | The GOVERN function's suggested actions read like an operating-model checklist |
| 4 | [IAPP third-party resources for AI governance](https://iapp.org/resources/article/third-party-resources-ai-governance) | IAPP | A curated list of frameworks and tools; useful alongside your AIGP study |

stops.title: Interview questions
stops.contentMd:
## Interview questions

| Question | Crisp answer |
| --- | --- |
| How would you build AI governance from scratch? | Discover (inventory, interviews, baseline), quick wins (acceptable use, interim approvals), design (policy, tiering, RACI, committee, templates), pilot on real use cases, then scale with a roadmap. |
| Centralised, federated or hub-and-spoke? | Hub-and-spoke for most large firms: central standards and high-risk approval, trained champions in each unit. Justify by size and maturity. |
| Why separate policy and standards? | The policy is stable and board-approved; standards hold thresholds that change often. |
| What goes in an AI inventory? | Owner, purpose, model type, vendor, data, risk tier, status, last review date. |
| What does a steering committee decide? | Policy and standards, Tier 1 approvals, above-appetite risk acceptance, escalations, and ethical refusals. |
| How do you stop governance being a bottleneck? | Tiering, fast lanes for low risk, embedding in existing processes, published turnaround times, champions. |
| How do you run a maturity assessment? | Agree scope, gather evidence including live walkthroughs, score domains 1-5 against criteria, find root causes, build a roadmap. |
| How do you measure if governance works? | Coverage, intake-to-decision time, shadow AI found, overdue actions, incidents, training, projects changed by governance. |
| What's the most common failure? | A framework nobody uses, because the approved route is slower than going around it. |

quiz.question: How would you build AI governance from scratch?
quiz.answer: Discover (inventory, interviews, baseline), quick wins (acceptable use, interim approvals), design (policy, tiering, RACI, committee, templates), pilot on real use cases, then scale with a roadmap.
quiz.explanation: The same 5-phase arc as the 90-day worked example — know it as a sequence, not just a list of parts.

quiz.question: Centralised, federated, or hub-and-spoke?
quiz.answer: Hub-and-spoke for most large firms: central standards and high-risk approval, with trained champions in each business unit. Justify the choice by the client's size and maturity.
quiz.explanation: Never give this answer without the justification clause — picking a model without reasoning sounds memorised.

quiz.question: Why separate policy and standards?
quiz.answer: The policy is stable and needs board approval; standards hold thresholds and technical requirements that change often, so you aren't back at the board every quarter.
quiz.explanation: A clean two-speed design: slow-changing governance vs fast-changing detail.

quiz.question: What goes in an AI inventory?
quiz.answer: Owner, purpose, model type, vendor, data, risk tier, status, and last review date.
quiz.explanation: The inventory is the foundation every other operating-model block depends on.

quiz.question: What does a steering committee decide?
quiz.answer: Policy and standards, Tier 1 use case approvals, above-appetite risk acceptance, escalations, and refusals made on ethical grounds.
quiz.explanation: The explicit ethical-refusal power is easy to forget but important to name — without it, the committee defers to legality every time.

quiz.question: How do you stop governance being a bottleneck?
quiz.answer: Tiering, fast lanes for low-risk cases, embedding intake into existing processes, published turnaround times, and trained champions in each unit.
quiz.explanation: A bottleneck is one of the two classic committee failure modes — know the fix cold.

quiz.question: How do you run a maturity assessment?
quiz.answer: Agree scope, gather evidence including live walkthroughs of real use cases, score each domain 1-5 against agreed criteria, find root causes behind the symptoms, then build a roadmap.
quiz.explanation: Walkthroughs are what separates a real maturity assessment from a paper-based gap check.

quiz.question: How do you measure whether governance actually works?
quiz.answer: Coverage, intake-to-decision time, shadow AI found, overdue actions, incidents, training completion, and projects changed or stopped by governance.
quiz.explanation: The last metric — projects actually changed or stopped — is the strongest signal the committee has real teeth.

quiz.question: What's the most common operating-model failure?
quiz.answer: A framework nobody uses, because the approved route is slower than just going around it.
quiz.explanation: Adoption has to be deliberately designed — proportionate tiers and fast lanes exist precisely to prevent this.

stops.title: Self-check
stops.contentMd:
## Self-check

Answer out loud before reading the answers.

1. Name six building blocks of an AI operating model.
2. What's the test of a good operating model?
3. Two ways a steering committee fails, and the fix for each.
4. What happens in weeks 9-12 of a 90-day plan?
5. Which metric shows whether the committee has teeth?

**Answers:** (1) Any six of: principles, policy, standards, procedures, inventory, intake, tiering, lifecycle gates, assessment templates, control library, monitoring, training. (2) A new use case appears and everyone knows where it goes, who assesses, who approves and how long it takes. (3) Rubber stamp, fixed by an explicit power to refuse and challenge; bottleneck, fixed by tiering and a fast-track route. (4) Pilot the process on 3 use cases, refine it, draft the control library, training plan and roadmap. (5) Projects changed or stopped by governance.

quiz.question: Name six building blocks of an AI operating model.
quiz.answer: Any six of: principles, policy, standards, procedures, inventory, intake, tiering, lifecycle gates, assessment templates, control library, monitoring, training.
quiz.explanation: There are 12 total in the module — six solidly recalled is enough for this check.

quiz.question: What's the test of a good operating model?
quiz.answer: A new use case appears and everyone knows where it goes, who assesses it, who can approve it, and how long that takes.
quiz.explanation: If people can't answer this quickly, they'll route around governance entirely.

quiz.question: Name two ways a steering committee fails, and the fix for each.
quiz.answer: Rubber stamp (approves everything, never challenges) — fixed by giving it an explicit power to refuse and challenge. Bottleneck (everything waits for a monthly meeting) — fixed by tiering, so only Tier 1 reaches the committee, plus a fast-track route.
quiz.explanation: These are the two opposite failure modes — too passive, or too slow.

quiz.question: What happens in weeks 9-12 of a 90-day plan?
quiz.answer: The pilot phase: run the full process on 3 use cases of different tiers, refine it, then draft the control library, training plan and roadmap.
quiz.explanation: This is where the designed process gets tested against real cases before scaling.

quiz.question: Which metric shows whether the committee has teeth?
quiz.answer: Projects changed or stopped by governance.
quiz.explanation: A committee that never changes or stops anything is, by definition, a rubber stamp.

stops.artifactPrompt: Write out your answers to all 5 self-check questions before revealing them. Note which ones you got wrong or hesitated on, and why.
